subject: axolotl
pitch:
Category: Animal.
Subject: axolotl with frilly pink gills.
Style: chibi.
reasoning:
I'm planning the axolotl model's design: a chibi proportioned creature with a wide smiling mouth, six gill fronds, stubby legs, and a finned tail, scaled down to about 0.3 meters long and 0.12 meters tall, facing forward and standing on the ground.

Now I'm working through the skeleton structure, placing the hip root joint and building a spine chain with catmull points running from tail to neck, then adding head and jaw joints with specific positions and hinge directions for a wide flat head shape and a separate lower jaw part.

I'm calculating vertical positions carefully so the body parts rest naturally near the floor -- checking that the body, head, jaw, and feet ellipsoids all have their bottoms sitting close to ground level without clipping, adjusting centers and radii for each part to make the proportions look right.

For the head, I'm sizing a flattened sphere and considering flat shading for a low-poly faceted look. For the eyes, I'm planning simple dark spheres with white highlight spheres placed on the head's surface rather than using decals, keeping the approach straightforward.

Adding blush decals, a smile curve, nostril dots, then painting the body pale leucistic pink with sparse darker freckles and a lighter belly tone before sweeping the body shape along the spine.

Now I'm setting up the skeleton: a tail chain with four joints branching off the hips, and a spine chain running forward through the pelvis toward the neck, placing hind legs near the hip joint.

For the body mesh, I'm sweeping a single catmull-rom path from the tail tip through the hips to the neck, binding it to the tail and spine bones so deformation follows the skeleton along its full length.

I'll size the radii narrow near the tail and gradually widen toward the body center, then plan a separate thin extruded fin outline for the tail membrane rather than trying to bake it into the main body radius.

Still shaping the fin geometry...

Still shaping fin outline... I'll give the tail fin a lighter pink shading with frilled edges, keeping the body countershaded, then move on to building stubby four-legged limbs with toes starting from the shoulder joints.

For the arms I'm setting up a bone chain from shoulder to elbow to wrist, sweeping a tapered radius along it, then capping each hand with a flat ellipsoid and adding four small capsule-shaped toes fanned out at the wrist tip.

I'm also settling on a side convention where s=1 maps to left (+X) and naming joints accordingly, then laying out rear leg joint positions similarly to the front legs but with thicker, more angled hip-knee-ankle placement.

For gills, I'm planning three stalks per side emerging from the back of the head, sweeping outward/upward/back as curves with frill cards along their length, starting from a base point on the head surface.

Setting up gill stalks as bezier sweeps colored deep pink, rigged as bone chains parented to the head for fan-like articulation, with each gill getting three joints across six total gills for flexible animation.

For the feathery frill detail, I'm planning to place card-based filament textures along each stalk using outward-facing frames from the sweep, positioning pairs of tapered spikes or leaf shapes on opposite sides of each gill to create a fuzzy, feathery silhouette.

So face normal points along flow, meaning the card lies perpendicular to the stalk like a flat disc fanning outward, with width along the binormal. With lean applied this reads more like a leaf tilted off the stalk rather than edge-on, so I'm reconsidering making flow align with the binormal instead.

Actually a simpler approach might be to abandon flat cards altogether and use spike/cone primitives extruded along a tilted direction, blending the normal and tangent vectors to get the leaning effect.

I'm placing spikes around each stalk at four angular positions across multiple cross-sections, keeping the total part count well under budget, and considering small sphere beads at the frond tips for detail. I'm also thinking about adding a thin flat fan shape for extra texture variety.

Now I'm working out the filament lengths so they taper from base to tip, and positioning the eyes as small decals on the upper skull using azimuth and elevation angles to get a chibi-style axolotl look.

For the eye decal, I'm casting a ray from the head center outward to hit the ellipsoid surface, then orienting the decal's normal to match that hit point to avoid z-fighting on the smooth-shaded head sphere. I'm also placing a smile decal lower on the head front, near the jawline, accounting for the ellipsoid's vertical radius to position the mouth correctly.

I'm now working out the lower jaw sphere's scale and vertical placement so it sits just below the head without creating a visible gap, using a pale belly color to differentiate it.

Adjusting head joint position, then adding facial details: cheek blush decals with pink ellipses, tiny dark nostril spheres near the front top, and scattered freckles across the back using a surface scatter function.

Now setting up body paint with countershaded skin tone, pink freckle spots, and a belly color transition, applying the same paint scheme to the head for consistency.

I'm defining colors for legs and toes with pale pastel tones, gill gradients from magenta stalks to lighter pink filament tips, and building the eye as a layered SVG with dark iris circles and two highlight dots for a glossy chibi look.

Now I'm sketching the smile as a curved stroke path with slight corner dimples, the blush as a striped ellipse, and setting up helper functions for side naming and toe placement based on wrist position, joint direction, and count.

Working out the toe geometry, I'm computing tip positions by rotating an outward direction vector by a spread angle, then building capsule bones from wrist to tip with small lighter-colored sphere bulbs at the ends, plus a palm sphere at the wrist. For the arm, I'm defining a catmull-rom path through three points to create a two-span chain with named joints for the arm role.

Now I'm placing specific joint coordinates for the front legs (shoulder, elbow, wrist) and hind legs, checking that the shoulder sits inside the body radius, and adjusting sweep radii so the leg tubes taper reasonably without poking through the body. I'm also setting up the hip joint and connecting it to tail and spine chains, with the body sweep extending to where the head sphere will cover the front end.

I'm defining the spine chain path and verifying the body radius taper along its length puts the belly just slightly off the ground, which seems fine for an axolotl-style stance since the lowest points (toes, jaw) still clear the floor.

Now checking total height with gills included—about 0.19 at gill tips versus 0.133 for head top. I'm setting up gill stalk positions with root and tip coordinates for each gill, using a bezier curve with an upward-bulging control point, fanning the three gills out behind the head with tips angled backward and outward.

Next I'm figuring out the frill row angles around the tube opening, setting up degree positions for the sides.

Then I'm sketching a chain bone structure for the head, with a fan role sweeping a stalk shape through three resampled points. For the filaments, I'm looping through several segments with increasing offset along the length, scaling each one's size down as it goes toward the tip, adjusting proportions for a chibi-style bigger look.

Working out the spike geometry and tip bead placement, figuring out how to anchor the tip sphere to the sweep's final point so it aligns correctly with the chain's end frame.

Beyond that, I decide extras like glow effects or bubbles aren't needed and skip them, focusing instead on freckle placement using the body surface normals to orient small cylindrical studs, and setting up decal targeting by sampling hit points on the skull surface using azimuth/elevation coordinates.

Now I'm working through the tail fin geometry — defining its extrusion parameters (position, thickness, bevel, bone attachment) and carefully laying out the outline points so the top and bottom edges taper smoothly toward the tail tip without self-intersecting.

Still writing fin ray paint logic...
